And we should remember too the truth of Paul's words
(Rom. I: 20) to the effect that the invisible being of God,
i.e. His eternal power and deity, is clearly perceptible in the
works of God or the creation of the world.
If this were not so, how could we as Christians delight in
this poetry which expresses the joy of springtime and the
religious feelings it awakens, and how could we delight in the
singing of these songs? On the contrary, as Christians we
can do this all the more fervently, in spite of the fact that
for the Christian man this kind of natural joy has a character-
istic limit.
However, before we speak of this we will further consider
why we can justifiably describe this feeling for nature as
piety; why we feel justified in saying that the God to whom
the human heart is here outpoured in yearning and thank-
fulness, is our God.
Man's characteristic estrangement from God consists in
this: that he thinks he has the reins of his life in his own
hands, that he thinks he can carve out his way in life through
his own initiative and planning, and by his own integrity
and achievement can securely lay the foundations of his
worth. It is just this arrogant attitude which is dissolved
when he opens his heart to the impact of nature.
Man can do many things. He can harness the forces of
nature to his own service, although he can only do so in so
far as he observes, and adapts himself to, the laws which
govern them. But he can wield not the slightest influence
over the great law of growth and ripening, birth and death,
change and decay. "While the earth remains ..." such is
the inflexible law of God which no man can alter. No man
can either arrest or hasten the great rhythm of the seasons;
no man can control the weather; no man is lord of life and
death. Man knows this very well; but in the busy activities
of daily life with its plans and its cares he usually forgets it
and deals with nature, with its resources and energies, as
